title: For Such a Time as This
summary: When Haman's decree to destroy the Jews is published, Mordecai and Jews across the empire go into mourning, fasting, and sackcloth. Through the eunuch Hathach, Mordecai urges Esther to plead with the king, and when she explains the danger of approaching him unsummoned, he warns her that silence will not save her. Esther calls for a three-day fast and resolves to go to the king, saying “And if I perish, I perish!”
story: Chapter 3 ended with Haman's edict sent to every province and with the king and Haman sitting down to drink while the city of Susa was thrown into confusion. Esther, now queen, has kept her Jewish identity hidden on Mordecai's instruction (2:10, 20). This chapter is the hinge of the book. Up to now Esther has been passive, taken into the palace and moved by others; here she becomes the one who decides and commands. The whole rescue that follows depends on the choice she makes at the end of this chapter, and the question Mordecai asks her, whether she has come to the kingdom for such a time as this, is the question the book's hidden providence invites every reader to ask.
historical:
The king of the story is Ahasuerus, the Hebrew form of the Persian name known in Greek as Xerxes, who ruled the Persian Empire from 486 to 465 BC. Esther became queen in his seventh year (2:16), about 479 BC, and Haman cast the lot in his twelfth year (3:7), about 474 BC. The action is set in Susa, one of the empire's royal capitals, in what is now southwestern Iran, where Darius I had built a great palace. Many Jews had remained in the eastern lands after Cyrus allowed exiles to return to Judah in 539/538 BC, and the book assumes they were scattered across the provinces from India to Cush.

The rule Esther describes, that anyone who came to the king in the inner court without being called would be put to death unless he held out his gold scepter, fits what Greek writers such as Herodotus say about the seclusion of Persian kings, who were approached through officials and ceremony. Reliefs from the Persian palace at Persepolis show the king enthroned and holding a long scepter as an official is presented to him. That Esther had not been called for thirty days suggests that her standing with an unpredictable king was uncertain, which makes her risk real.
cultural:
Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth and ashes were the ordinary signs of grief and humiliation in Israel and among its neighbors. Sackcloth was a coarse cloth, often of goat hair, and ashes on the head showed a person brought low. Fasting went with mourning and with urgent prayer. Mordecai cannot pass the king's gate in sackcloth, because signs of mourning were kept out of the royal presence, where the king was to be surrounded by joy.

The chapter also depends on the world of the Persian harem. Esther cannot simply walk out to meet Mordecai; she communicates through eunuchs, royal servants assigned to the women's quarters, and messages pass back and forth several times. Hathach becomes the go-between on whom a nation's survival hangs. Esther's call for a fast of three days, night and day, without food or drink, is severe, and in the Old Testament fasting nearly always accompanies prayer, so a first reader would assume the Jews of Susa were praying, even though the book does not say so. Many Jewish communities later marked a fast before Purim, known as the Fast of Esther, remembering this chapter.
literary: The chapter is built as an exchange of messages, with Hathach carrying words back and forth between the palace and the square. Each round raises the stakes: Mordecai's lament, Esther's gift of clothes refused, Mordecai's report and the copy of the decree, Esther's objection, Mordecai's warning, and Esther's decision. The climax falls in two short speeches. Mordecai's reply (verses 13-14) is the book's clearest statement of its outlook, and famously it never names God, speaking only of relief and deliverance that will “arise from another place.” Esther's answer turns her from the one who receives instructions into the one who gives them, and the chapter ends with a reversal of roles: Mordecai goes and does all that Esther instructed him.

outline.t: Mordecai and the Jews mourn the decree
Esther learns the news through Hathach
Esther explains the law of the inner court
Esther calls a fast and resolves to go to the king

doctrines.note: Mordecai's words assume that deliverance will come even if Esther fails, and that her position may have been arranged for this very moment. The book teaches God's providence without naming God, by showing events that are ordered toward the rescue of his people.

The fast Esther calls is the chapter's form of prayer. In the Old Testament fasting is joined to crying out to God, and the Jews' mourning across the provinces and Esther's three-day fast show a people bringing their need before the one who can save.
Esther's resolve is faith that acts without guarantees. She does not know how the king will receive her, and she accepts that she may die, but she goes because her people's lives are at stake.

words.note: Hatstsalah, deliverance, rescue. The noun appears only here in the Old Testament, though it comes from a common verb meaning to snatch away or rescue. Mordecai is certain that deliverance will come; what is uncertain is whether Esther will be part of it.

Et, time, a set or fitting moment. Mordecai's question turns on this word: Esther's rise to the throne may have been for such a time as this. The word is common, but here it carries the sense of a moment appointed for action, the thing the whole book shows being arranged behind the scenes.

Tsum, to fast. Esther tells the Jews of Susa to fast for her, and she and her maidens will fast too. Fasting in Scripture is a bodily act of humility and urgent seeking, usually tied to repentance, grief, or prayer in crisis.

Charash, to be silent or keep quiet. If Esther remains silent at this time, Mordecai says, she and her father's house will perish. The book's drama turns on when to speak and when to keep silent: Esther once kept her identity quiet, and now silence would be deadly.

christ: Esther stands before a king with power of life and death, risking her own life to plead for her people, and the pattern of a mediator who goes in on behalf of others runs through the Bible to Jesus. The link is thematic, not a prediction: the book of Esther never points forward to a Messiah. But the New Testament presents Christ as the one who did what Esther could only risk, laying down his life for his people, and because of him believers are told something Esther could not have imagined of the Persian throne: “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). Mordecai's confidence that deliverance would come from another place also fits the Bible's larger testimony that God keeps his promises to his people even when human instruments falter.

hard.q: Why doesn't this chapter, the book's turning point, mention God or prayer at all?
hard.a: Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible besides the Song of Songs that never mentions God, and its silence is most striking here, where Mordecai speaks of relief from another place and Esther calls a fast without any word about prayer. Readers have explained this in several ways. Many see the silence as deliberate: the book shows God working hiddenly through ordinary choices and apparent coincidences, as he often seems to work in a world where he is not seen. Some suggest that a book meant to be read at a boisterous festival, or one written for Jews living under a foreign empire, spoke about God with reserve. Others think the phrase another place is itself a reverent way of pointing to God without naming him, though some scholars read it as meaning only another human source of help. The Greek translation of Esther adds long prayers by Mordecai and Esther and names God often, which shows that ancient readers also felt the silence. What the Hebrew text does is leave the reader to see the hand that the characters do not name.

questions: Mordecai tells Esther that her privileged position won't protect her. Where might comfort or status tempt you to stay silent about someone else's danger?
Esther asks others to fast for her before she acts. What does it look like to seek the support of a community before a costly decision?
Mordecai asks whether Esther came to the kingdom for such a time as this. How might you read your own circumstances differently if you believed they were not accidental?
